newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll lead to test French left on Europe, economy.
newsitem.headline: Poll lead to test French left on Europe, economy.

text.p: The French lefts surprise lead in Sunday's first-round parliamentary elections will force it to address issues it fudged early in the campaign -- bridging yawning gaps on Europe and economic policy to share power.

Projections broadcast after polling ended at 1800 GMT showed the opposition Socialists, Communists, extreme-left and other left candidates set to capture between 40.6 and 41.6 percent of the vote, with the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate right candidates scoring between 36.1 and 37.1 percent.
Two opinion poll institutes forecast the RPR-UDF coalition winning fewer than the 289 seats required for a National Assembly majority.

While transfer voting in France's two-round polling system makes it hard to extrapolate from a first-round lead, the left is now in with a real chance of victory if it can convince voters it could govern coherently.
Forming a coalition government could prove a formidable challenge.

First there is a duel over the extent to which the senior partners, the Socialists, will call the shots in government and how much they are willing to concede both in terms of general policy and key posts.
Then, there is the reality of reconciling their most blatant rift -- over the European Union's planned single currency, the euro.

The Communist party opposes Economic and Monetary Union and wants a fresh referendum on the euro, but the Socialists back a single currency, albeit with conditions such as creating a political counterweight to the future European central bank.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has said the Socialists would set the line and the Communists would have to toe it if they wanted cabinet seats. Communist leader Robert Hue responded by rejecting any bid to impose hegemony on the left.
On national economic policy, the Communist party is far more doggedly opposed to the privatisation of state enterprises and in some cases is in favour of re-nationalisation.
The Socialists have given mixed signals which hint that they are at least willing to consider sales of minority stakes in state firms like France Telecom to the private sector.

On unemployment, currently running at a post-war record 12.8 percent, both parties have ambitious goals for creating jobs with help from the state, but they may well not see eye-to-eye on the pace of action or how they raise the money to pay for it.

The Socialists promise to create 350,000 jobs in the public sector funded mainly by the abolition of ineffective existing employment incentive schemes, and to push for the creation of an equal number of jobs in the private sector.
During the campaign, Jospin extended the target period for creating those 700,000 youth jobs from two years to three. The Communists want to create 1.5 million jobs in two years.

The Communists want to boost purchasing power by raising wages, notably with an immediate 1,000-franc ($175) increase in the 6,400-franc ($1,122) a month minimum wage. Jospin is much more cautious on wages, calling for sector negotiations.

Both sides say cutting value-added tax is a priority on the grounds that weak consumer spending is the Achilles heel of the economy, but the Communists are also openly calling for big hikes in wealth tax and a tax on financial market earnings.
Their clearest division is on European monetary union, which the Communists say rides roughshod over social policy in the sole interests of "King money" and the financial markets.
Hue and Jospin glossed over the issue in a joint declaration issued within days of President Jacques Chirac's decision to call a snap election.

Rejecting any further austerity measures, the declaration spoke of the need to "go beyond the Maastricht treaty", noting the two parties had taken opposite sides in France's 1992 referendum on monetary union.
Jospin later insisted the Socialists would make no concession on supporting the euro.
"There won't be both a 'Yes' and a 'No' to the single currency. There will be a single line, the one which we propose to the French people," he said.

"I told Robert Hue that if there is a majority in which the Socialists have a far bigger contingent than the Communist party...there can only be one line: the one set by the French people which gave the parliamentary majority to the candidates of this party," he said.
